## Summary

v8 should time sung lines in seconds rather than bars, give each section a four-bar plan, and let phrases stretch, shrink or overlap at the rates real songs use. Placement should choose the best setting by weighted rules instead of dying when no setting is perfect. All four placement failures of songs 54 to 56 come from v7 fixing a line's length in bars before the words are known.

- **The research record.** Theory treats bars as beats of a larger metre, which listeners infer from repetition and harmony. Rothstein's expansions and overlaps let phrases bend over it. Hayes's text-setting model treats placing words as weighing competing rules, learned from singers.

- **Pop.** The average bar is about two seconds at any time signature (de Clercq 2016). Four-bar groups are the norm, and real songs expand, elide and insert bars freely. Metric irregularities cluster at section joins, and country is the most regular genre.

- **Measured here, on 9,313 lines in 198 charting songs:**

   - Slow songs give a line fewer bars. Lines of 6 to 8 syllables take one bar 36% of the time in slow songs against 6% in fast ones, while slots in seconds change much less.

   - One-bar lines have spans that grow with their syllables.

   - Rests inside a line stay under a beat and a half.

   - Sung lines overlap the harmony's four-bar groups with long pickups.

- **For v8:** slots in seconds; the felt tempo chosen at intake; phrase operators drawn at kept rates; placement by weighted rules. These would close 749.25, 749.30 and 749.31, and let song 56 run at ♩ = 72.

## What Luthier v7 does above the bar now

v7 measures beats inside a bar well, and phrase lengths as counts. But it has no model of strong and weak bars, of how a phrase can stretch, shrink or overlap, or of a tempo felt in half time. Lines are placed into fixed slots of one, two or four bars, and when the words do

### not fit, the build dies.

|Item|Where in v7|What it does|Its limit|
|---|---|---|---|
|Beat weight inside the bar|Window 47; the Longuet-Higgins and Lee weights|Sixteenth-note weights for syncopation|Stops at the bar line; the word "hypermeter" appears nowhere in the spec|
|A line's slot|27.41, fix 230 (Window 117)|From syllables: one or two bars up to 5, two bars for 6 to 8, four bars from 9; a three-bar slot (8% of kept lines) only by design; a section's slots must sum to a multiple of four|Slots are set in the song's file, not drawn; nothing says which bar of a four-bar group is strong|
|Where a line starts and lands|27.41, fix 231|55% of pop lines start with a pickup, 20% on the downbeat; the last stress lands on beat 1 in 23%, beat 3 in 20%, off the beat in 38%|Shares within the bar only|
|Odd lengths|Window 37|31% of chart sections are not a multiple of four bars; 21% of phrases are odd; offered as departures (a 9-bar chorus, a 6-bar bridge, a 2/4 bar before the chorus)|A menu the writer picks from, priced in departure units; nothing writes them|
|Section lengths|Windows 29, 41|Sections of eight bars; the first chorus near bar 20|Counts, not a phrase grammar|
|Felt tempo|Window 131|Admits a song felt in half time would move its tempo bands|Not modelled; song 56 at♩= 72 had to be written at 144 with a half-time feel|

### **Where songs 54 to 56 broke.**

- **Song 54 (749.25).** Two-thirds of builds died for want of a placement, on 9- and 10syllable lines in two-bar slots with borrowed rhythms.

- **Song 55 (749.30).** 678 of 1,000 builds died, 591 of them at the chorus's one-bar lines of 4 to 6 syllables.

- **Song 55 (749.31).** The survivors included short lines spread over two bars with a rest of three and a half beats in the middle.

- **Song 56.** At ♩ = 72 with a line a bar, every one of 40 test builds died; it ran only at double tempo.

All four are the same gap: a line's length in bars is fixed before the words are known, and nothing above the bar lets it stretch, shrink or overlap the next phrase.

## The academic record: hypermeter, phrase rhythm, text-setting

Theory treats the bars of a phrase as beats of a larger metre. Phrases can stretch, overlap or shrink against that larger metre without breaking it. And setting words to a rhythm is a trade-off between rules, not a fit-or-fail test.

- **The metric hierarchy has limits in time.** London's _Hearing in Time_ sets metric entrainment between about [100 milliseconds and 5 to 6 seconds](https://academic.oup.com/book/11161/chapter/159624475). A four-bar group at pop tempos (6 to 9 seconds) is above that. So hypermeter is learned and inferred from repetition and harmony, not felt as a beat.

- **Phrase rhythm.** Rothstein's _Phrase Rhythm in Tonal Music_ (1989) separates the regular hypermeter from the phrases laid over it. Phrases can be expanded internally or at their ends, or overlap so a bar ends one phrase and begins the next. An overlap can delete a bar from the pattern and shift strong and weak bars [(study notes on Rothstein)](https://www.scribd.com/document/334395558/Rothstein-Phrase-Rhythm). Temperley (2008) adds the hypermetrical transition, a gradual shift from odd-strong to even-strong bars ([as summarised by Bakulina](https://www.mtosmt.org/ojs/index.php/mto/article/view/63/97)).

- **Hypermeter is a learned expectation.** Love (2015) models hypermeter as a momentto-moment expectation of two- and four-bar units, felt as accent, surprise, confusion, tension and relief, and recognised only after the cues have passed ([MTO](https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.15.21.3/mto.15.21.3.love.php)).

- **Metric dissonance.** Krebs's two kinds, carried into rock by Biamonte: _displacement_ (a unit starts a slot early or late) and _grouping_ (units bundled differently, as in a hemiola) [(Biamonte 2014](https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.14.20.2/mto.14.20.2.biamonte.php)).

**Text-setting as weighing rules.** Halle and Lerdahl (1993) posed the problem: singers given a new verse for a known tune agree where its syllables go. [Hayes (2009)](https://linguistics.ucla.edu/people/hayes/BrownMinicourse/HayesSwarthmorePresentation.pdf) models it as weighted constraints on a 16-position grid for a four-beat line:

   - stress on strong positions;

   - phrase-final stresses on strong beats;

   - strong positions filled, weak ones left empty, pauses at line edges;

   - no run of three empty positions;

   - long syllables on strong positions.

- Weights learned from 425 folk-song lines chanted by English speakers predict their choices at r .88, and each singer's own weights pick that singer's favourite setting.

- **Pop text-setting is sensitive to syllable length.** Ryan (2022), on [2,371 English pop songs,](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/english-language-and-linguistics/article/abs/syllable-weight-and-natural-duration-in-textsetting-popular-music-in-english/50F8885341914C37D6F1BD22A632A0B6) finds the grid placement follows syllables' natural duration, beyond the lengthening at phrase ends.

For the engine, the text-setting work is the most directly useful. It describes placing a line as a choice among settings that each break some rules, scored by weights learned from songs. v7's placement instead fails when no setting satisfies every rule at once.

## Metre in popular song

Pop works in four-bar groups and an average bar of about two seconds. It stretches, cuts and overlaps phrases freely, and much of its metric irregularity sits at section boundaries.

- **The two-second bar.** [de Clercq (2016)](https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.16.22.3/mto.16.22.3.declercq.php), across three rock and chart corpora:

- Songs in four average about 120 beats a minute and songs in 6/8 about 60, so the average bar is about 2 seconds either way.

- A bar should be read where the harmony and melody move, near 2 seconds, not where the drum pattern says.

- Half-time is common in R&B and southern rap, double-time in metal and punk.

- The same song can be drummed at very different speeds while its bars stay similar in length: one song's two versions differ about sixfold in drum speed but only threefold in bar length.

In his country examples, a ballad near 72 beats a minute changes chord every two bars.

**Four-bar groups, by repetition.** Pop organises into quadruple hypermetre more often than not, and Temperley found half the chords on odd-numbered downbeats are the tonic ([Fink 2023,](https://core-prod.cambridgecore.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/22D74F53CFF118FFF2545ACE5172A212/S026114302300048Xa.pdf/the-anchoring-vi-schema-and-its-relation-to-phrase-rhythm-in-popular-music.pdf) citing Stephenson 2002 and Temperley 2018). Open Music Theory's example: a four-bar chord loop sets the hypermeter ([Open Music Theory)](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/hypermeter_v2).

- **Expansion, elision and insertion in real songs.** Fink's cases include:

- an eight-bar chorus whose last bar doubles as the next unit's first;

- a harmony held on IV as a written-out pause;

- a slowed harmonic rhythm making a verse 17 bars;

- a chorus rerouted by V of vi and stretched to 11 bars;

- a 23-bar verse built on a 16-bar phrase with an inserted passage;

- a final chorus that drops four bars and adds a coda.

**Metric dissonance, mostly at boundaries.** Biamonte (2014) finds small-scale dissonances at openings, cadences and transitions, the commonest being a partial bar at a section join. Larger ones mark contrast, as in loose verses against tight choruses. About two-thirds of Beatles songs are in plain 4/4; country and songs with tambourine are the most regular; and dissonance rises over each band's career and across the decades [(MTO)](https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.14.20.2/mto.14.20.2.biamonte.php). Biamonte's chapter adds pre-choruses that drop to half time and shortened bars that drive into the next section ([Routledge Companion)](https://music.arts.uci.edu/abauer/6.2/readings/Routledge_Companion_Popular_Music_Analysis__Biamonte_rhythmic_fctns-13_chapter.pdf).

- **Odd lengths are ordinary.** v7's Window 37 already counts them: 31% of chart sections are not a multiple of four bars, and 71% of songs have at least one.

## Measured here: how real songs place their lines

Real songs time a line in seconds, not bars. A slow song gives a line of the same length fewer bars, so its bars carry more syllables. v7's slot table is in bars at every tempo. Song 56's lines of 9 to 11 syllables in a 3.3-second bar ask about 3 syllables a second, inside what real slow songs sing (median 2.8, upper quartile 3.5), yet the bar-based table ruled the one-bar slot out.

![Slow songs give a line fewer bars: lines are timed in seconds](data:image/png;base64,)

*CoCoPops Billboard (CC BY-NC 4.0): studies/metre/metre_results.json*

**The data.** CoCoPops Billboard: 198 charting songs in 4/4 (1959 to 1991) with melody, syllables, sections and chord timestamps; 9,313 sung lines. A line starts at a capitalised syllable or after two beats of silence; its slot runs to the next line's first syllable (Window 117's rules).

||Fast songs (bar under 1.8 s)|Middle|Slow songs (bar 2.6 s or more)|
|---|---|---|---|
|Songs / lines|75 / 3,419|98 / 4,277|25 / 1,244|
|6 to 8 syllables in one bar or less|6%|22%|36%|
|9 or more syllables in one bar or less|0%|1%|9%|
|9 or more syllables in four bars or more|51%|36%|18%|
|Median slot in seconds, 6 to 8 / 9 or more syllables|3.2 / 4.6|3.6 / 5.1|4.1 / 5.8|
|Syllables a second while singing (median)|3.45|3.14|2.81|

### What else the lines show:

- **The bar.** A median 1.91 seconds (quartiles 1.67 and 2.32), close to de Clercq's twosecond bar; 13% of songs have bars of 2.6 seconds or more. Song 56's bar at ♩ = 72 is 3.33 seconds.

- **Pickups.** 85% of verse lines and 80% of chorus lines start off the downbeat, more than Window 117's 55% because a start anywhere after beat 1 counts here.

- **One-bar lines.** 36% of lines take a bar or less; they hold a median 3 syllables (90th percentile 6), and 7% hold 7 or more. Their sung span grows with syllables: 1.5 beats for 3, 2.5 for 5, 3.25 for 7, 3.5 for 8 (medians). These are the spans a one-bar draw needs (749.30).

- **Rests inside a line.** The longest rest inside a line has a 90th percentile of half a beat to a beat and a half, by syllables and slot. A silence of two beats or more is where transcribers start a new line, so song 55's rests of three and a half beats read as two lines, not one (749.31).

- **Lines against the four-bar group.** In 8- and 16-bar sections, chords put the tonic on bar 1 of the four-bar group 55% of the time (bar 3, 43%). Sung lines begin mostly in bars 3 and 4 (58%) as long pickups into the next group, and bar 3 holds the fewest sung notes (20%). The voice's phrases overlap the harmonic groups rather than sitting inside them.

- **Odd sections.** 33% of verse, chorus, pre-chorus and bridge sections are not a multiple of four bars, matching Window 37.

Cautions: these are 1959 to 1991 hits transcribed by experts; tempo is read from chord timestamps; and the line rule cannot see a long rest inside a line, so the inner-rest figures are a floor.

## What this means for v8: a layer above the bar

v8 should time lines in seconds, give each section a four-bar plan, and let phrases stretch, shrink or overlap by measured rates. Placement should weigh competing rules and choose the best setting, not die when no setting is perfect.

1. **Slots in seconds, not bars.** A line's slot comes from its syllables and the song's bar length, using the kept table above: in a slow song, 6 to 8 syllables take one bar 36% of the time, and 9 or more take two bars at the median. The singing rate stays inside kept quartiles for the tempo band (about 2.3 to 4.2 syllables a second). This replaces fix 230's bar-based defaults and would have let song 56 run at ♩ = 72.

2. **The felt tempo is chosen, not patched.** At intake the engine picks the bar level nearest two seconds where the harmony moves (de Clercq 2016) and records halftime or double-time as a feel. The double-tempo workaround of songs 51 and 56 becomes a setting.

3. **A four-bar plan per section.**

   - Harmony marks bars 1 and 3 of each group (the tonic on bar 1 in 55% of kept groups).

   - Sung lines lie across the groups with long pickups (80% to 85% start off the downbeat), many entering in bars 3 and 4.

A breath falls near bar 3.

4. **Phrase operators, at kept rates.** Before a build fails, the placer may: add a bar at a phrase's end, making a 5-bar phrase or a 9- or 10-bar chorus; overlap a phrase's last bar with the next phrase's first;

   - hold a chord a bar longer inside the phrase;

   - split a long line into two;

drop a half bar at a section join.

Window 37's rates set how often each may occur (31% of sections and 21% of phrases are odd), and Fink's and Rothstein's cases give the shapes. These are drawn by the engine, not picked from a menu.

5. **Placement by weighted rules.** Score every candidate setting of a line by Hayes's rules: stress on strong positions, phrase-final stress on strong beats, strong positions filled, no lapse of three empty positions, long syllables on strong positions. Learn the weights from kept lines and keep the best setting, as the melody judge already chooses among survivors.

6. **The three open findings, closed with these numbers.**

   - 749.30: a one-bar line's span comes from its syllables (median 1.5 beats for 3 syllables to 3.5 for 8).

   - 749.31: a rest inside a line is capped at the kept 90th percentile (half a beat to a beat and a half); a gap of two beats makes two lines.

   - 749.25: a borrowed rhythm that cannot take a line's syllables splits notes or redraws, as operator 4 allows.

7. **Metric dissonance as a chosen tool.** The shortened bar at a section join, the half-time pre-chorus and the cadential hemiola are offered by genre and section role. Country is the most regular genre (Biamonte), so its songs get few.

### **Tests.**

- (a) Songs 54, 55 and 56 run with placement deaths under one build in ten, song 56 at ♩ = 72 without the double-tempo trick.

- (b) Every v8 song's slots, by tempo band, fall inside the kept quartiles in seconds.

- (c) Odd phrases and sections appear at kept rates across a run.

- (d) Weighted placement predicts held-out kept settings better than the current rules.

- (e) The no-hand-input test: slots come from the lyric and tempo, not typed per song.

**Still open.** No perception study of hypermeter in pop turned up. The kept data on line placement is 1959 to 1991 chart songs; Hooktheory's lead sheets would add recent songs if they can be fetched again.

## Files and sources

The scripts and results are in the repo under `studies/metre` (commit c3f7fdc): `lines_cocopops.py` and `metre_test.py` , with `metre_results.json` . The CoCoPops data is not kept in the repo; the README says how to fetch it. This study follows [the tension study.](https://claude.ai/artifact/HQvP9aJ1NUS4ApTWRm3wTS)
